{{Citation needed|date=November 2007}} {{Otheruses}} '''Sanka''' (山窩) also known as Japanese Gypsies were a group of itinerant people in Japan who were said to have lived without permanent settlements.<ref>[https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sanka-people Sanka | African, Animist & Nomadic | Britannica]</ref>
== Lifestyle == Sanka were said to have lived a [[hunter-gatherer society|hunter-gatherer]] lifestyle, moving from place to place. They were known for producing [[winnowing baskets]] and would visit villages to trade their goods. There were occupational distinctions within the Sanka community. Those called "Pon" engaged in river fishing and performed secondary tasks such as [[bamboo crafts]]<ref>{{Cite book|author=Tsutsui Isao|title=The Origins of Sanka: From Kugutsu to the Korean Peninsula|publisher=Kawade Shobo Shinsha|year=2012|isbn=978-4-309-22578-4|chapter=1. Ecological Theories of Sanka (Regional Nomenclature and Characteristics)}}</ref>. Another subgroup, referred to as "Minaoshi" or "Tenba," made winnowing baskets, [[sasara]], and [[brooms]], and earned their income through
peddling and repairs.
In the Meiji period, the Sanka population was estimated at around 200,000, and about 10,000 were thought to remain immediately after World War II. However, these numbers are speculative and have not been verified. Women in Sanka communities reportedly often resorted to prostitution to sustain themselves, leading to the term "Sanka" being associated with prostitutes. While the Sanka predominantly spoke Japanese, they also used a distinct [[Sanka language]] for certain terms.
== Nomenclature == The term "Sanka" was written using various kanji characters, such as 山窩, 山家, 三家, 散家, 傘下, or 燦下. These characters were often phonetic or descriptive, with some suggesting meanings such as "people who live under umbrellas or the sky instead of houses." Regional variations in terminology included "Pon," "Kametsuri," "Minaoshi" (箕直), "Mitsukuri" (箕作), and "Tenba" (転場). These terms often reflected specific trades or practices within the Sanka community.
=== Government and Police Terminology === * '''Government:''' The term "Sanka" was used to categorize itinerants as part of the "vagrants" or "wandering nonpersons" groups. * '''Police:''' The police uniformly referred to them as "Yamaka" (山窩), labeling them as "criminal groups of wandering units." * '''Researchers:''' Scholars used the term "Sanka" distinctly to separate it from police classifications. * '''Forestry Department:''' The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry used "Sanka" or "Yamaka" to document individuals as part of forest preservation efforts against illegal logging.
Some sources suggest that the Sanka referred to themselves as "Kenta" to denote their community. Groups camping by rivers were called "Seburi Kenta," while those with fixed abodes were known as "Doyatsuke Kenta"<ref name="Sanka Self-Naming">{{Cite book|author=Nobuyoshi Wada|title=Dark Street Life: Dictionary of Slang and Symbols|publisher=Toa Shobo|year=1936|url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/10297894}}</ref>.
== History of the Term "Sanka" == {{Original research|date=October 2020}} The earliest appearance of the term "Sanka" in records dates to the late [[Edo period]]. [[Matsuura Takeshirō]], an explorer known for naming [[Hokkaido]], recorded being saved by the Sanka in his writings. However, this term was not self-applied by the group, and its use likely predated these documents. In [[Hiroshima Prefecture]], an 1855 village document used "Sanka" to describe "mountain-dwelling criminals."
During the [[Meiji era]], "Yamaka" became a term frequently used in police and administrative documents to describe a group akin to [[bandits]]. Folklorist [[Kunio Yanagita]] conducted research into "Yamaka" during this period, documenting his findings. By the [[Second World War]], references to the term "Yamaka" in official documents had largely disappeared.
The term gained widespread recognition postwar through the fictionalized "Sanka novels" of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]]. These novels popularized Sanka as a subject of intrigue, blending folklore with drama. Writers such as [[Hiroyuki Itsuki]] further fictionalized the Sanka, incorporating fantastical elements. Movies like ''[[Seburi Monogatari]]'' (directed by [[Sadao Nakajima]]) were also inspired by these stories.
The [[occult]] boom of the 1980s brought renewed interest in the Sanka, with sensational claims linking them to [[kamiyo moji]] (ancient script), [[supernatural powers]], and [[ancient civilizations]]. These claims fueled skepticism, leading some to question whether the Sanka ever existed.
== Research == The first academic investigation into the Sanka was conducted by [[Kunio Yanagita]]. Between 1911 and 1912, he published a series of articles titled "Itaka and Sanka" in the journal ''Anthropological Magazine''<ref name="yanagida1">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=6|pages=332–338|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.332}}</ref><ref name="yanagida2">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka (Part 2)|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=8|pages=465–471|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.465}}</ref>. Yanagita criticized earlier theories that equated Sanka with criminality, arguing that their actions reflected differing views on property rather than innate criminality.
Subsequent research, including the work of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]], contributed to the popular image of the Sanka, though much of it was later revealed to be fictionalized.
== Sanka in Media == * ''[[Seburi Monogatari]]'' (1985 film by [[Sadao Nakajima]]) * ''[[The Last News]]'' - Features a story of a Sanka descendant seeking revenge. * ''[[Mushishi]]'' - Introduces a group called "Watari." * ''[[Jigokuraku]]'' - Features descendants of the Sanka. * ''[[Pearl Wolf]]'' - Includes a subplot involving Sanka lineage.
== References == {{Reflist}}
== Further Reading == * [[Isao Tsutsui]], ''The Origins of Sanka'', Kawade Shobo Shinsha, 2012. * [[Hiroshi Itsuki]], ''The Phantom Wandering People: Sanka'', Bungeishunju, 2001. == See Also == * [[Romani people]] * [[Itinerant groups in Japan]] * [[Kunio Yanagita]]

{{Citation needed|date=November 2007}} {{Otheruses}} '''Sanka''' (山窩) also known as Japanese Gypsies were a group of itinerant people in Japan who were said to have lived without permanent settlements.<ref>[https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sanka-people Sanka | African, Animist & Nomadic | Britannica]</ref>
== Lifestyle == Sanka were said to have lived a [[hunter-gatherer society|hunter-gatherer]] lifestyle, moving from place to place. They were known for producing [[winnowing baskets]] and would visit villages to trade their goods. There were occupational distinctions within the Sanka community. Those called "Pon" engaged in river fishing and performed secondary tasks such as [[bamboo crafts]]<ref>{{Cite book|author=Tsutsui Isao|title=The Origins of Sanka: From Kugutsu to the Korean Peninsula|publisher=Kawade Shobo Shinsha|year=2012|isbn=978-4-309-22578-4|chapter=1. Ecological Theories of Sanka (Regional Nomenclature and Characteristics)}}</ref>. Another subgroup, referred to as "Minaoshi" or "Tenba," made winnowing baskets, [[sasara]], and [[brooms]], and earned their income through
peddling and repairs.
In the Meiji period, the Sanka population was estimated at around 200,000, and about 10,000 were thought to remain immediately after World War II. However, these numbers are speculative and have not been verified. Women in Sanka communities reportedly often resorted to prostitution to sustain themselves, leading to the term "Sanka" being associated with prostitutes. While the Sanka predominantly spoke Japanese, they also used a distinct [[Sanka language]] for certain terms.
== Nomenclature == The term "Sanka" was written using various kanji characters, such as 山窩, 山家, 三家, 散家, 傘下, or 燦下. These characters were often phonetic or descriptive, with some suggesting meanings such as "people who live under umbrellas or the sky instead of houses." Regional variations in terminology included "Pon," "Kametsuri," "Minaoshi" (箕直), "Mitsukuri" (箕作), and "Tenba" (転場). These terms often reflected specific trades or practices within the Sanka community.
=== Government and Police Terminology === * '''Government:''' The term "Sanka" was used to categorize itinerants as part of the "vagrants" or "wandering nonpersons" groups. * '''Police:''' The police uniformly referred to them as "Yamaka" (山窩), labeling them as "criminal groups of wandering units." * '''Researchers:''' Scholars used the term "Sanka" distinctly to separate it from police classifications. * '''Forestry Department:''' The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry used "Sanka" or "Yamaka" to document individuals as part of forest preservation efforts against illegal logging.
Some sources suggest that the Sanka referred to themselves as "Kenta" to denote their community. Groups camping by rivers were called "Seburi Kenta," while those with fixed abodes were known as "Doyatsuke Kenta"<ref name="Sanka Self-Naming">{{Cite book|author=Nobuyoshi Wada|title=Dark Street Life: Dictionary of Slang and Symbols|publisher=Toa Shobo|year=1936|url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/10297894}}</ref>.

[[Matsuura Takeshirō]], an explorer known for naming [[Hokkaido]], recorded being saved by the Sanka in his writings. However, this term was not self-applied by the group, and its use likely predated these documents. In [[Hiroshima Prefecture]], an 1855 village document used "Sanka" to describe "mountain-dwelling criminals."
During the [[Meiji era]], "Yamaka" became a term frequently used in police and administrative documents to describe a group akin to [[bandits]]. Folklorist [[Kunio Yanagita]] conducted research into "Yamaka" during this period, documenting his findings. By the [[Second World War]], references to the term "Yamaka" in official documents had largely disappeared.
The term gained widespread recognition postwar through the fictionalized "Sanka novels" of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]]. These novels popularized Sanka as a subject of intrigue, blending folklore with drama. Writers such as [[Hiroyuki Itsuki]] further fictionalized the Sanka, incorporating fantastical elements. Movies like ''[[Seburi Monogatari]]'' (directed by [[Sadao Nakajima]]) were also inspired by these stories.
The [[occult]] boom of the 1980s brought renewed interest in the Sanka, with sensational claims linking them to [[kamiyo moji]] (ancient script), [[supernatural powers]], and [[ancient civilizations]]. These claims fueled skepticism, leading some to question whether the Sanka ever existed.

Yanagita criticized earlier theories that equated Sanka with criminality, arguing that their actions reflected differing views on property rather than innate criminality.
Subsequent research, including the work of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]], contributed to the popular image of the Sanka, though much of it was later revealed to be fictionalized.
== Sanka in Media == * ''[[Seburi Monogatari]]'' (1985 film by [[Sadao Nakajima]]) * ''[[The Last News]]'' - Features a story of a Sanka descendant seeking revenge. * ''[[Mushishi]]'' - Introduces a group called "Watari." * ''[[Jigokuraku]]'' - Features descendants of the Sanka. * ''[[Pearl Wolf]]'' - Includes a subplot involving Sanka lineage.

Those called "Pon" engaged in river fishing and performed secondary tasks such as [[bamboo crafts]]<ref>{{Cite book|author=Tsutsui Isao|title=The Origins of Sanka: From Kugutsu to the Korean Peninsula|publisher=Kawade Shobo Shinsha|year=2012|isbn=978-4-309-22578-4|chapter=1. Ecological Theories of Sanka (Regional Nomenclature and Characteristics)}}</ref>. Another subgroup, referred to as "Minaoshi" or "Tenba," made winnowing baskets, [[sasara]], and [[brooms]], and earned their income through
peddling and repairs.
In the Meiji period, the Sanka population was estimated at around 200,000, and about 10,000 were thought to remain immediately after World War II. However, these numbers are speculative and have not been verified. Women in Sanka communities reportedly often resorted to prostitution to sustain themselves, leading to the term "Sanka" being associated with prostitutes. While the Sanka predominantly spoke Japanese, they also used a distinct [[Sanka language]] for certain terms.
== Nomenclature == The term "Sanka" was written using various kanji characters, such as 山窩, 山家, 三家, 散家, 傘下, or 燦下. These characters were often phonetic or descriptive, with some suggesting meanings such as "people who live under umbrellas or the sky instead of houses." Regional variations in terminology included "Pon," "Kametsuri," "Minaoshi" (箕直), "Mitsukuri" (箕作), and "Tenba" (転場). These terms often reflected specific trades or practices within the Sanka community.
=== Government and Police Terminology === * '''Government:''' The term "Sanka" was used to categorize itinerants as part of the "vagrants" or "wandering nonpersons" groups. * '''Police:''' The police uniformly referred to them as "Yamaka" (山窩), labeling them as "criminal groups of wandering units." * '''Researchers:''' Scholars used the term "Sanka" distinctly to separate it from police classifications. * '''Forestry Department:''' The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry used "Sanka" or "Yamaka" to document individuals as part of forest preservation efforts against illegal logging.
Some sources suggest that the Sanka referred to themselves as "Kenta" to denote their community. Groups camping by rivers were called "Seburi Kenta," while those with fixed abodes were known as "Doyatsuke Kenta"<ref name="Sanka Self-Naming">{{Cite book|author=Nobuyoshi Wada|title=Dark Street Life: Dictionary of Slang and Symbols|publisher=Toa Shobo|year=1936|url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/10297894}}</ref>.
== History of the Term "Sanka" == {{Original research|date=October 2020}} The earliest appearance of the term "Sanka" in records dates to the late [[Edo period]]. [[Matsuura Takeshirō]], an explorer known for naming [[Hokkaido]], recorded being saved by the Sanka in his writings. However, this term was not self-applied by the group, and its use likely predated these documents. In [[Hiroshima Prefecture]], an 1855 village document used "Sanka" to describe "mountain-dwelling criminals."
During the [[Meiji era]], "Yamaka" became a term frequently used in police and administrative documents to describe a group akin to [[bandits]]. Folklorist [[Kunio Yanagita]] conducted research into "Yamaka" during this period, documenting his findings. By the [[Second World War]], references to the term "Yamaka" in official documents had largely disappeared.
The term gained widespread recognition postwar through the fictionalized "Sanka novels" of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]]. These novels popularized Sanka as a subject of intrigue, blending folklore with drama. Writers such as [[Hiroyuki Itsuki]] further fictionalized the Sanka, incorporating fantastical elements. Movies like ''[[Seburi Monogatari]]'' (directed by [[Sadao Nakajima]]) were also inspired by these stories.
The [[occult]] boom of the 1980s brought renewed interest in the Sanka, with sensational claims linking them to [[kamiyo moji]] (ancient script), [[supernatural powers]], and [[ancient civilizations]]. These claims fueled skepticism, leading some to question whether the Sanka ever existed.
== Research == The first academic investigation into the Sanka was conducted by [[Kunio Yanagita]]. Between 1911 and 1912, he published a series of articles titled "Itaka and Sanka" in the journal ''Anthropological Magazine''<ref name="yanagida1">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=6|pages=332–338|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.332}}</ref><ref name="yanagida2">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka (Part 2)|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=8|pages=465–471|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.465}}</ref>. Yanagita criticized earlier theories that equated Sanka with criminality, arguing that their actions reflected differing views on property rather than innate criminality.
Subsequent research, including the work of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]], contributed to the popular image of the Sanka, though much of it was later revealed to be fictionalized.
== Sanka in Media == * ''[[Seburi Monogatari]]'' (1985 film by [[Sadao Nakajima]]) * ''[[The Last News]]'' - Features a story of a Sanka descendant seeking revenge. * ''[[Mushishi]]'' - Introduces a group called "Watari." * ''[[Jigokuraku]]'' - Features descendants of the Sanka. * ''[[Pearl Wolf]]'' - Includes a subplot involving Sanka lineage.

== Lifestyle == Sanka were said to have lived a [[hunter-gatherer society|hunter-gatherer]] lifestyle, moving from place to place. They were known for producing [[winnowing baskets]] and would visit villages to trade their goods. There were occupational distinctions within the Sanka community. Those called "Pon" engaged in river fishing and performed secondary tasks such as [[bamboo crafts]]<ref>{{Cite book|author=Tsutsui Isao|title=The Origins of Sanka: From Kugutsu to the Korean Peninsula|publisher=Kawade Shobo Shinsha|year=2012|isbn=978-4-309-22578-4|chapter=1. Another subgroup, referred to as "Minaoshi" or "Tenba," made winnowing baskets, [[sasara]], and [[:en:brooms|brooms]], and earned their income through
peddling and repairs.
In the Meiji period, the Sanka population was estimated at around 200,000, and about 10,000 were thought to remain immediately after World War II. However, these numbers are speculative and have not been verified. <!--Sanka--><!--Sanka--> [[Category:Japanese legends]] [[Category:Burakumin]] [[Category:Folklore studies]] <!--jawiki derived wikidata interwikis--> [[en:Sanka (ethnic group)]] [[ko:산카]] [[tr:Sankalar]] [[zh:山窩]]

{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q4833074]] Wikidata name: Sankas [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:05, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Citation needed|date=November 2007}} {{Otheruses}} '''Sanka''' (山窩) also known as Japanese Gypsies were a group of itinerant people in Japan who were said to have lived without permanent settlements.<ref>[https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sanka-people Sanka | African, Animist & Nomadic | Britannica]</ref>
== Lifestyle == Sanka were said to have lived a [[:en:hunter-gatherer society|hunter-gatherer]] lifestyle, moving from place to place. They were known for producing [[winnowing baskets]] and would visit villages to trade their goods. There were occupational distinctions within the Sanka community. Those called "Pon" engaged in river fishing and performed secondary tasks such as [[bamboo crafts]]<ref>{{Cite book|author=Tsutsui Isao|title=The Origins of Sanka: From Kugutsu to the Korean Peninsula|publisher=Kawade Shobo Shinsha|year=2012|isbn=978-4-309-22578-4|chapter=1. Ecological Theories of Sanka (Regional Nomenclature and Characteristics)}}</ref>. Another subgroup, referred to as "Minaoshi" or "Tenba," made winnowing baskets, [[:en:Sasara|Sasara]], and [[:en:brooms|brooms]], and earned their income through
peddling and repairs.
In the Meiji period, the Sanka population was estimated at around 200,000, and about 10,000 were thought to remain immediately after World War II. However, these numbers are speculative and have not been verified. Women in Sanka communities reportedly often resorted to prostitution to sustain themselves, leading to the term "Sanka" being associated with prostitutes. While the Sanka predominantly spoke Japanese, they also used a distinct [[Sanka language]] for certain terms.
== Nomenclature == The term "Sanka" was written using various kanji characters, such as 山窩, 山家, 三家, 散家, 傘下, or 燦下. These characters were often phonetic or descriptive, with some suggesting meanings such as "people who live under umbrellas or the sky instead of houses." Regional variations in terminology included "Pon," "Kametsuri," "Minaoshi" (箕直), "Mitsukuri" (箕作), and "Tenba" (転場). These terms often reflected specific trades or practices within the Sanka community.
=== Government and Police Terminology === * '''Government:''' The term "Sanka" was used to categorize itinerants as part of the "vagrants" or "wandering nonpersons" groups. * '''Police:''' The police uniformly referred to them as "Yamaka" (山窩), labeling them as "criminal groups of wandering units." * '''Researchers:''' Scholars used the term "Sanka" distinctly to separate it from police classifications. * '''Forestry Department:''' The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry used "Sanka" or "Yamaka" to document individuals as part of forest preservation efforts against illegal logging.
Some sources suggest that the Sanka referred to themselves as "Kenta" to denote their community. Groups camping by rivers were called "Seburi Kenta," while those with fixed abodes were known as "Doyatsuke Kenta"<ref name="Sanka Self-Naming">{{Cite book|author=Nobuyoshi Wada|title=Dark Street Life: Dictionary of Slang and Symbols|publisher=Toa Shobo|year=1936|url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/10297894}}</ref>.
== History of the Term "Sanka" == {{Original research|date=October 2020}} The earliest appearance of the term "Sanka" in records dates to the late [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. [[:en:Matsuura Takeshirō|Matsuura Takeshirō]], an explorer known for naming [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]], recorded being saved by the Sanka in his writings. However, this term was not self-applied by the group, and its use likely predated these documents. In [[:en:Hiroshima Prefecture|Hiroshima Prefecture]], an 1855 village document used "Sanka" to describe "mountain-dwelling criminals."
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], "Yamaka" became a term frequently used in police and administrative documents to describe a group akin to [[:en:Bandits|Bandits]]. Folklorist [[Kunio Yanagita]] conducted research into "Yamaka" during this period, documenting his findings. By the [[:en:Second World War|Second World War]], references to the term "Yamaka" in official documents had largely disappeared.
The term gained widespread recognition postwar through the fictionalized "Sanka novels" of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]]. These novels popularized Sanka as a subject of intrigue, blending folklore with drama. Writers such as [[:en:Hiroyuki Itsuki|Hiroyuki Itsuki]] further fictionalized the Sanka, incorporating fantastical elements. Movies like ''[[:en:Seburi Monogatari|Seburi Monogatari]]'' (directed by [[:en:Sadao Nakajima|Sadao Nakajima]]) were also inspired by these stories.
The [[:en:Occult|Occult]] boom of the 1980s brought renewed interest in the Sanka, with sensational claims linking them to [[:en:kamiyo moji|kamiyo moji]] (ancient script), [[:en:supernatural powers|supernatural powers]], and [[:en:ancient civilizations|ancient civilizations]]. These claims fueled skepticism, leading some to question whether the Sanka ever existed.
== Research == The first academic investigation into the Sanka was conducted by [[Kunio Yanagita]]. Between 1911 and 1912, he published a series of articles titled "Itaka and Sanka" in the journal ''Anthropological Magazine''<ref name="yanagida1">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=6|pages=332–338|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.332}}</ref><ref name="yanagida2">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka (Part 2)|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=8|pages=465–471|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.465}}</ref>. Yanagita criticized earlier theories that equated Sanka with criminality, arguing that their actions reflected differing views on property rather than innate criminality.
Subsequent research, including the work of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]], contributed to the popular image of the Sanka, though much of it was later revealed to be fictionalized.
== Sanka in Media == * ''[[:en:Seburi Monogatari|Seburi Monogatari]]'' (1985 film by [[:en:Sadao Nakajima|Sadao Nakajima]]) * ''[[The Last News]]'' - Features a story of a Sanka descendant seeking revenge. * ''[[:en:Mushishi|Mushishi]]'' - Introduces a group called "Watari." * ''[[:en:Jigokuraku|Jigokuraku]]'' - Features descendants of the Sanka. * ''[[Pearl Wolf]]'' - Includes a subplot involving Sanka lineage.
== References == {{Reflist}}
== Further Reading == * [[Isao Tsutsui]], ''The Origins of Sanka'', Kawade Shobo Shinsha, 2012. * [[:en:Hiroshi Itsuki|Hiroshi Itsuki]], ''The Phantom Wandering People: Sanka'', Bungeishunju, 2001. == See Also == * [[:en:Romani people|Romani people]] * [[Itinerant groups in Japan]] * [[Kunio Yanagita]]

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Sanka (ethnic group)]][[ja:サンカ]][[ko:산카]][[th:ซังกะ]][[tr:Sankalar]][[zh:山窩]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q4833074]] Wikidata name: Sankas [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:05, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Citation needed|date=November 2007}} {{Otheruses}} '''Sanka''' (山窩) also known as Japanese Gypsies were a group of itinerant people in Japan who were said to have lived without permanent settlements.<ref>[https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sanka-people Sanka | African, Animist & Nomadic | Britannica]</ref>
== Lifestyle == Sanka were said to have lived a [[:en:hunter-gatherer society|hunter-gatherer]] lifestyle, moving from place to place. They were known for producing [[winnowing baskets]] and would visit villages to trade their goods. There were occupational distinctions within the Sanka community. Those called "Pon" engaged in river fishing and performed secondary tasks such as [[bamboo crafts]]<ref>{{Cite book|author=Tsutsui Isao|title=The Origins of Sanka: From Kugutsu to the Korean Peninsula|publisher=Kawade Shobo Shinsha|year=2012|isbn=978-4-309-22578-4|chapter=1. Ecological Theories of Sanka (Regional Nomenclature and Characteristics)}}</ref>. Another subgroup, referred to as "Minaoshi" or "Tenba," made winnowing baskets, [[:en:Sasara|Sasara]], and [[:en:brooms|brooms]], and earned their income through
peddling and repairs.
In the Meiji period, the Sanka population was estimated at around 200,000, and about 10,000 were thought to remain immediately after World War II. However, these numbers are speculative and have not been verified. Women in Sanka communities reportedly often resorted to prostitution to sustain themselves, leading to the term "Sanka" being associated with prostitutes. While the Sanka predominantly spoke Japanese, they also used a distinct [[Sanka language]] for certain terms.
== Nomenclature == The term "Sanka" was written using various kanji characters, such as 山窩, 山家, 三家, 散家, 傘下, or 燦下. These characters were often phonetic or descriptive, with some suggesting meanings such as "people who live under umbrellas or the sky instead of houses." Regional variations in terminology included "Pon," "Kametsuri," "Minaoshi" (箕直), "Mitsukuri" (箕作), and "Tenba" (転場). These terms often reflected specific trades or practices within the Sanka community.
=== Government and Police Terminology === * '''Government:''' The term "Sanka" was used to categorize itinerants as part of the "vagrants" or "wandering nonpersons" groups. * '''Police:''' The police uniformly referred to them as "Yamaka" (山窩), labeling them as "criminal groups of wandering units." * '''Researchers:''' Scholars used the term "Sanka" distinctly to separate it from police classifications. * '''Forestry Department:''' The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry used "Sanka" or "Yamaka" to document individuals as part of forest preservation efforts against illegal logging.
Some sources suggest that the Sanka referred to themselves as "Kenta" to denote their community. Groups camping by rivers were called "Seburi Kenta," while those with fixed abodes were known as "Doyatsuke Kenta"<ref name="Sanka Self-Naming">{{Cite book|author=Nobuyoshi Wada|title=Dark Street Life: Dictionary of Slang and Symbols|publisher=Toa Shobo|year=1936|url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/10297894}}</ref>.
== History of the Term "Sanka" == {{Original research|date=October 2020}} The earliest appearance of the term "Sanka" in records dates to the late [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. [[:en:Matsuura Takeshirō|Matsuura Takeshirō]], an explorer known for naming [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]], recorded being saved by the Sanka in his writings. However, this term was not self-applied by the group, and its use likely predated these documents. In [[:en:Hiroshima Prefecture|Hiroshima Prefecture]], an 1855 village document used "Sanka" to describe "mountain-dwelling criminals."
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], "Yamaka" became a term frequently used in police and administrative documents to describe a group akin to [[:en:Bandits|Bandits]]. Folklorist [[Kunio Yanagita]] conducted research into "Yamaka" during this period, documenting his findings. By the [[:en:Second World War|Second World War]], references to the term "Yamaka" in official documents had largely disappeared.
The term gained widespread recognition postwar through the fictionalized "Sanka novels" of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]]. These novels popularized Sanka as a subject of intrigue, blending folklore with drama. Writers such as [[:en:Hiroyuki Itsuki|Hiroyuki Itsuki]] further fictionalized the Sanka, incorporating fantastical elements. Movies like ''[[:en:Seburi Monogatari|Seburi Monogatari]]'' (directed by [[:en:Sadao Nakajima|Sadao Nakajima]]) were also inspired by these stories.
The [[:en:Occult|Occult]] boom of the 1980s brought renewed interest in the Sanka, with sensational claims linking them to [[:en:kamiyo moji|kamiyo moji]] (ancient script), [[:en:supernatural powers|supernatural powers]], and [[:en:ancient civilizations|ancient civilizations]]. These claims fueled skepticism, leading some to question whether the Sanka ever existed.
== Research == The first academic investigation into the Sanka was conducted by [[Kunio Yanagita]]. Between 1911 and 1912, he published a series of articles titled "Itaka and Sanka" in the journal ''Anthropological Magazine''<ref name="yanagida1">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=6|pages=332–338|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.332}}</ref><ref name="yanagida2">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka (Part 2)|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=8|pages=465–471|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.465}}</ref>. Yanagita criticized earlier theories that equated Sanka with criminality, arguing that their actions reflected differing views on property rather than innate criminality.
Subsequent research, including the work of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]], contributed to the popular image of the Sanka, though much of it was later revealed to be fictionalized.
== Sanka in Media == * ''[[:en:Seburi Monogatari|Seburi Monogatari]]'' (1985 film by [[:en:Sadao Nakajima|Sadao Nakajima]]) * ''[[The Last News]]'' - Features a story of a Sanka descendant seeking revenge. * ''[[:en:Mushishi|Mushishi]]'' - Introduces a group called "Watari." * ''[[:en:Jigokuraku|Jigokuraku]]'' - Features descendants of the Sanka. * ''[[Pearl Wolf]]'' - Includes a subplot involving Sanka lineage.
== References == {{Reflist}}
== Further Reading == * [[Isao Tsutsui]], ''The Origins of Sanka'', Kawade Shobo Shinsha, 2012. * [[:en:Hiroshi Itsuki|Hiroshi Itsuki]], ''The Phantom Wandering People: Sanka'', Bungeishunju, 2001. == See Also == * [[:en:Romani people|Romani people]] * [[Itinerant groups in Japan]] * [[Kunio Yanagita]]

In the Meiji period, the Sanka population was estimated at around 200,000, and about 10,000 were thought to remain immediately after World War II. However, these numbers are speculative and have not been verified. Women in Sanka communities reportedly often resorted to prostitution to sustain themselves, leading to the term "Sanka" being associated with prostitutes. While the Sanka predominantly spoke Japanese, they also used a distinct [[Sanka language]] for certain terms.
== Nomenclature == The term "Sanka" was written using various kanji characters, such as 山窩, 山家, 三家, 散家, 傘下, or 燦下. These characters were often phonetic or descriptive, with some suggesting meanings such as "people who live under umbrellas or the sky instead of houses." Regional variations in terminology included "Pon," "Kametsuri," "Minaoshi" (箕直), "Mitsukuri" (箕作), and "Tenba" (転場). These terms often reflected specific trades or practices within the Sanka community.
=== Government and Police Terminology === * '''Government:''' The term "Sanka" was used to categorize itinerants as part of the "vagrants" or "wandering nonpersons" groups. * '''Police:''' The police uniformly referred to them as "Yamaka" (山窩), labeling them as "criminal groups of wandering units." * '''Researchers:''' Scholars used the term "Sanka" distinctly to separate it from police classifications. * '''Forestry Department:''' The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry used "Sanka" or "Yamaka" to document individuals as part of forest preservation efforts against illegal logging.
Some sources suggest that the Sanka referred to themselves as "Kenta" to denote their community. Groups camping by rivers were called "Seburi Kenta," while those with fixed abodes were known as "Doyatsuke Kenta"<ref name="Sanka Self-Naming">{{Cite book|author=Nobuyoshi Wada|title=Dark Street Life: Dictionary of Slang and Symbols|publisher=Toa Shobo|year=1936|url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/10297894}}</ref>.
== History of the Term "Sanka" == {{Original research|date=October 2020}} The earliest appearance of the term "Sanka" in records dates to the late [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. [[:en:Matsuura Takeshirō|Matsuura Takeshirō]], an explorer known for naming [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]], recorded being saved by the Sanka in his writings. However, this term was not self-applied by the group, and its use likely predated these documents. In [[:en:Hiroshima Prefecture|Hiroshima Prefecture]], an 1855 village document used "Sanka" to describe "mountain-dwelling criminals."
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], "Yamaka" became a term frequently used in police and administrative documents to describe a group akin to [[:en:Bandits|Bandits]]. Folklorist [[Kunio Yanagita]] conducted research into "Yamaka" during this period, documenting his findings. By the [[:en:Second World War|Second World War]], references to the term "Yamaka" in official documents had largely disappeared.
The term gained widespread recognition postwar through the fictionalized "Sanka novels" of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]]. These novels popularized Sanka as a subject of intrigue, blending folklore with drama. Writers such as [[:en:Hiroyuki Itsuki|Hiroyuki Itsuki]] further fictionalized the Sanka, incorporating fantastical elements. Movies like ''[[:en:Seburi Monogatari|Seburi Monogatari]]'' (directed by [[:en:Sadao Nakajima|Sadao Nakajima]]) were also inspired by these stories.
The [[:en:Occult|Occult]] boom of the 1980s brought renewed interest in the Sanka, with sensational claims linking them to [[:en:kamiyo moji|kamiyo moji]] (ancient script), [[:en:supernatural powers|supernatural powers]], and [[:en:ancient civilizations|ancient civilizations]]. These claims fueled skepticism, leading some to question whether the Sanka ever existed.
== Research == The first academic investigation into the Sanka was conducted by [[Kunio Yanagita]]. Between 1911 and 1912, he published a series of articles titled "Itaka and Sanka" in the journal ''Anthropological Magazine''<ref name="yanagida1">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=6|pages=332–338|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.332}}</ref><ref name="yanagida2">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka (Part 2)|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=8|pages=465–471|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.465}}</ref>. Yanagita criticized earlier theories that equated Sanka with criminality, arguing that their actions reflected differing views on property rather than innate criminality.
Subsequent research, including the work of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]], contributed to the popular image of the Sanka, though much of it was later revealed to be fictionalized.
== Sanka in Media == * ''[[:en:Seburi Monogatari|Seburi Monogatari]]'' (1985 film by [[:en:Sadao Nakajima|Sadao Nakajima]]) * ''[[The Last News]]'' - Features a story of a Sanka descendant seeking revenge. * ''[[:en:Mushishi|Mushishi]]'' - Introduces a group called "Watari." * ''[[:en:Jigokuraku|Jigokuraku]]'' - Features descendants of the Sanka. * ''[[Pearl Wolf]]'' - Includes a subplot involving Sanka lineage.

== Further Reading == * [[Isao Tsutsui]], ''The Origins of Sanka'', Kawade Shobo Shinsha, 2012. * [[:en:Hiroshi Itsuki|Hiroshi Itsuki]], ''The Phantom Wandering People: Sanka'', Bungeishunju, 2001. == See Also == * [[:en:Romani people|Romani people]] * [[Itinerant groups in Japan]] * [[Kunio Yanagita]]

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Sanka (ethnic group)]][[ja:サンカ]][[ko:산카]][[th:ซังกะ]][[tr:Sankalar]][[zh:山窩]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Sanka (ethnic group)]][[ja:サンカ]][[ko:산카]][[th:ซังกะ]][[tr:Sankalar]][[zh:山窩]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q4833074]] Wikidata name: Sankas [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:05, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Citation needed|date=November 2007}} {{Otheruses}} '''Sanka''' (山窩) also known as Japanese Gypsies were a group of itinerant people in Japan who were said to have lived without permanent settlements.<ref>[https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sanka-people Sanka | African, Animist & Nomadic | Britannica]</ref>
== Lifestyle == Sanka were said to have lived a [[:en:hunter-gatherer society|hunter-gatherer]] lifestyle, moving from place to place. They were known for producing [[winnowing baskets]] and would visit villages to trade their goods. There were occupational distinctions within the Sanka community. Those called "Pon" engaged in river fishing and performed secondary tasks such as [[bamboo crafts]]<ref>{{Cite book|author=Tsutsui Isao|title=The Origins of Sanka: From Kugutsu to the Korean Peninsula|publisher=Kawade Shobo Shinsha|year=2012|isbn=978-4-309-22578-4|chapter=1. Ecological Theories of Sanka (Regional Nomenclature and Characteristics)}}</ref>. Another subgroup, referred to as "Minaoshi" or "Tenba," made winnowing baskets, [[:en:Sasara|Sasara]], and [[:en:brooms|brooms]], and earned their income through
peddling and repairs.
In the Meiji period, the Sanka population was estimated at around 200,000, and about 10,000 were thought to remain immediately after World War II. However, these numbers are speculative and have not been verified. Women in Sanka communities reportedly often resorted to prostitution to sustain themselves, leading to the term "Sanka" being associated with prostitutes. While the Sanka predominantly spoke Japanese, they also used a distinct [[Sanka language]] for certain terms.
== Nomenclature == The term "Sanka" was written using various kanji characters, such as 山窩, 山家, 三家, 散家, 傘下, or 燦下. These characters were often phonetic or descriptive, with some suggesting meanings such as "people who live under umbrellas or the sky instead of houses." Regional variations in terminology included "Pon," "Kametsuri," "Minaoshi" (箕直), "Mitsukuri" (箕作), and "Tenba" (転場). These terms often reflected specific trades or practices within the Sanka community.
=== Government and Police Terminology === * '''Government:''' The term "Sanka" was used to categorize itinerants as part of the "vagrants" or "wandering nonpersons" groups. * '''Police:''' The police uniformly referred to them as "Yamaka" (山窩), labeling them as "criminal groups of wandering units." * '''Researchers:''' Scholars used the term "Sanka" distinctly to separate it from police classifications. * '''Forestry Department:''' The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry used "Sanka" or "Yamaka" to document individuals as part of forest preservation efforts against illegal logging.
Some sources suggest that the Sanka referred to themselves as "Kenta" to denote their community. Groups camping by rivers were called "Seburi Kenta," while those with fixed abodes were known as "Doyatsuke Kenta"<ref name="Sanka Self-Naming">{{Cite book|author=Nobuyoshi Wada|title=Dark Street Life: Dictionary of Slang and Symbols|publisher=Toa Shobo|year=1936|url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/10297894}}</ref>.
== History of the Term "Sanka" == {{Original research|date=October 2020}} The earliest appearance of the term "Sanka" in records dates to the late [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. [[:en:Matsuura Takeshirō|Matsuura Takeshirō]], an explorer known for naming [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]], recorded being saved by the Sanka in his writings. However, this term was not self-applied by the group, and its use likely predated these documents. In [[:en:Hiroshima Prefecture|Hiroshima Prefecture]], an 1855 village document used "Sanka" to describe "mountain-dwelling criminals."
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], "Yamaka" became a term frequently used in police and administrative documents to describe a group akin to [[:en:Bandits|Bandits]]. Folklorist [[Kunio Yanagita]] conducted research into "Yamaka" during this period, documenting his findings. By the [[:en:Second World War|Second World War]], references to the term "Yamaka" in official documents had largely disappeared.
The term gained widespread recognition postwar through the fictionalized "Sanka novels" of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]]. These novels popularized Sanka as a subject of intrigue, blending folklore with drama. Writers such as [[:en:Hiroyuki Itsuki|Hiroyuki Itsuki]] further fictionalized the Sanka, incorporating fantastical elements. Movies like ''[[:en:Seburi Monogatari|Seburi Monogatari]]'' (directed by [[:en:Sadao Nakajima|Sadao Nakajima]]) were also inspired by these stories.
The [[:en:Occult|Occult]] boom of the 1980s brought renewed interest in the Sanka, with sensational claims linking them to [[:en:kamiyo moji|kamiyo moji]] (ancient script), [[:en:supernatural powers|supernatural powers]], and [[:en:ancient civilizations|ancient civilizations]]. These claims fueled skepticism, leading some to question whether the Sanka ever existed.
== Research == The first academic investigation into the Sanka was conducted by [[Kunio Yanagita]]. Between 1911 and 1912, he published a series of articles titled "Itaka and Sanka" in the journal ''Anthropological Magazine''<ref name="yanagida1">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=6|pages=332–338|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.332}}</ref><ref name="yanagida2">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka (Part 2)|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=8|pages=465–471|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.465}}</ref>. Yanagita criticized earlier theories that equated Sanka with criminality, arguing that their actions reflected differing views on property rather than innate criminality.
Subsequent research, including the work of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]], contributed to the popular image of the Sanka, though much of it was later revealed to be fictionalized.
== Sanka in Media == * ''[[:en:Seburi Monogatari|Seburi Monogatari]]'' (1985 film by [[:en:Sadao Nakajima|Sadao Nakajima]]) * ''[[The Last News]]'' - Features a story of a Sanka descendant seeking revenge. * ''[[:en:Mushishi|Mushishi]]'' - Introduces a group called "Watari." * ''[[:en:Jigokuraku|Jigokuraku]]'' - Features descendants of the Sanka. * ''[[Pearl Wolf]]'' - Includes a subplot involving Sanka lineage.

== Further Reading == * [[Isao Tsutsui]], ''The Origins of Sanka'', Kawade Shobo Shinsha, 2012. * [[:en:Hiroshi Itsuki|Hiroshi Itsuki]], ''The Phantom Wandering People: Sanka'', Bungeishunju, 2001. == See Also == * [[:en:Romani people|Romani people]] * [[Itinerant groups in Japan]] * [[Kunio Yanagita]]

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Sanka (ethnic group)]][[ja:サンカ]][[ko:산카]][[th:ซังกะ]][[tr:Sankalar]][[zh:山窩]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Sanka (ethnic group)]][[ja:サンカ]][[ko:산카]][[th:ซังกะ]][[tr:Sankalar]][[zh:山窩]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[en:Sanka (ethnic group)]][[ja:サンカ]][[ko:산카]][[th:ซังกะ]][[tr:Sankalar]][[zh:山窩]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q4833074]] Wikidata name: Sankas [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:05, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Citation needed|date=November 2007}} {{Otheruses}} '''Sanka''' (山窩) also known as Japanese Gypsies were a group of itinerant people in Japan who were said to have lived without permanent settlements.<ref>[https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sanka-people Sanka | African, Animist & Nomadic | Britannica]</ref>
== Lifestyle == Sanka were said to have lived a [[:en:hunter-gatherer society|hunter-gatherer]] lifestyle, moving from place to place. They were known for producing [[winnowing baskets]] and would visit villages to trade their goods. There were occupational distinctions within the Sanka community. Those called "Pon" engaged in river fishing and performed secondary tasks such as [[bamboo crafts]]<ref>{{Cite book|author=Tsutsui Isao|title=The Origins of Sanka: From Kugutsu to the Korean Peninsula|publisher=Kawade Shobo Shinsha|year=2012|isbn=978-4-309-22578-4|chapter=1. Ecological Theories of Sanka (Regional Nomenclature and Characteristics)}}</ref>. Another subgroup, referred to as "Minaoshi" or "Tenba," made winnowing baskets, [[:en:Sasara|Sasara]], and [[:en:brooms|brooms]], and earned their income through
peddling and repairs.
In the Meiji period, the Sanka population was estimated at around 200,000, and about 10,000 were thought to remain immediately after World War II. However, these numbers are speculative and have not been verified. Women in Sanka communities reportedly often resorted to prostitution to sustain themselves, leading to the term "Sanka" being associated with prostitutes. While the Sanka predominantly spoke Japanese, they also used a distinct [[Sanka language]] for certain terms.
== Nomenclature == The term "Sanka" was written using various kanji characters, such as 山窩, 山家, 三家, 散家, 傘下, or 燦下. These characters were often phonetic or descriptive, with some suggesting meanings such as "people who live under umbrellas or the sky instead of houses." Regional variations in terminology included "Pon," "Kametsuri," "Minaoshi" (箕直), "Mitsukuri" (箕作), and "Tenba" (転場). These terms often reflected specific trades or practices within the Sanka community.
=== Government and Police Terminology === * '''Government:''' The term "Sanka" was used to categorize itinerants as part of the "vagrants" or "wandering nonpersons" groups. * '''Police:''' The police uniformly referred to them as "Yamaka" (山窩), labeling them as "criminal groups of wandering units." * '''Researchers:''' Scholars used the term "Sanka" distinctly to separate it from police classifications. * '''Forestry Department:''' The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry used "Sanka" or "Yamaka" to document individuals as part of forest preservation efforts against illegal logging.
Some sources suggest that the Sanka referred to themselves as "Kenta" to denote their community. Groups camping by rivers were called "Seburi Kenta," while those with fixed abodes were known as "Doyatsuke Kenta"<ref name="Sanka Self-Naming">{{Cite book|author=Nobuyoshi Wada|title=Dark Street Life: Dictionary of Slang and Symbols|publisher=Toa Shobo|year=1936|url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/10297894}}</ref>.
== History of the Term "Sanka" == {{Original research|date=October 2020}} The earliest appearance of the term "Sanka" in records dates to the late [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. [[:en:Matsuura Takeshirō|Matsuura Takeshirō]], an explorer known for naming [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]], recorded being saved by the Sanka in his writings. However, this term was not self-applied by the group, and its use likely predated these documents. In [[:en:Hiroshima Prefecture|Hiroshima Prefecture]], an 1855 village document used "Sanka" to describe "mountain-dwelling criminals."
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], "Yamaka" became a term frequently used in police and administrative documents to describe a group akin to [[:en:Bandits|Bandits]]. Folklorist [[Kunio Yanagita]] conducted research into "Yamaka" during this period, documenting his findings. By the [[:en:Second World War|Second World War]], references to the term "Yamaka" in official documents had largely disappeared.
The term gained widespread recognition postwar through the fictionalized "Sanka novels" of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]]. These novels popularized Sanka as a subject of intrigue, blending folklore with drama. Writers such as [[:en:Hiroyuki Itsuki|Hiroyuki Itsuki]] further fictionalized the Sanka, incorporating fantastical elements. Movies like ''[[:en:Seburi Monogatari|Seburi Monogatari]]'' (directed by [[:en:Sadao Nakajima|Sadao Nakajima]]) were also inspired by these stories.
The [[:en:Occult|Occult]] boom of the 1980s brought renewed interest in the Sanka, with sensational claims linking them to [[:en:kamiyo moji|kamiyo moji]] (ancient script), [[:en:supernatural powers|supernatural powers]], and [[:en:ancient civilizations|ancient civilizations]]. These claims fueled skepticism, leading some to question whether the Sanka ever existed.
== Research == The first academic investigation into the Sanka was conducted by [[Kunio Yanagita]]. Between 1911 and 1912, he published a series of articles titled "Itaka and Sanka" in the journal ''Anthropological Magazine''<ref name="yanagida1">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=6|pages=332–338|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.332}}</ref><ref name="yanagida2">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka (Part 2)|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=8|pages=465–471|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.465}}</ref>. Yanagita criticized earlier theories that equated Sanka with criminality, arguing that their actions reflected differing views on property rather than innate criminality.
Subsequent research, including the work of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]], contributed to the popular image of the Sanka, though much of it was later revealed to be fictionalized.
== Sanka in Media == * ''[[:en:Seburi Monogatari|Seburi Monogatari]]'' (1985 film by [[:en:Sadao Nakajima|Sadao Nakajima]]) * ''[[The Last News]]'' - Features a story of a Sanka descendant seeking revenge. * ''[[:en:Mushishi|Mushishi]]'' - Introduces a group called "Watari." * ''[[:en:Jigokuraku|Jigokuraku]]'' - Features descendants of the Sanka. * ''[[Pearl Wolf]]'' - Includes a subplot involving Sanka lineage.
== References == {{Reflist}}
== Further Reading == * [[Isao Tsutsui]], ''The Origins of Sanka'', Kawade Shobo Shinsha, 2012. * [[:en:Hiroshi Itsuki|Hiroshi Itsuki]], ''The Phantom Wandering People: Sanka'', Bungeishunju, 2001. == See Also == * [[:en:Romani people|Romani people]] * [[Itinerant groups in Japan]] * [[Kunio Yanagita]]

peddling and repairs.

== Lifestyle == Sanka were said to have lived a [[:en:hunter-gatherer society|hunter-gatherer]] lifestyle, moving from place to place. They were known for producing [[winnowing baskets]] and would visit villages to trade their goods. There were occupational distinctions within the Sanka community. Those called "Pon" engaged in river fishing and performed secondary tasks such as [[bamboo crafts]]<ref>{{Cite book|author=Tsutsui Isao|title=The Origins of Sanka: From Kugutsu to the Korean Peninsula|publisher=Kawade Shobo Shinsha|year=2012|isbn=978-4-309-22578-4|chapter=1. Ecological Theories of Sanka (Regional Nomenclature and Characteristics)}}</ref>. Another subgroup, referred to as "Minaoshi" or "Tenba," made winnowing baskets, [[:en:Sasara|Sasara]], and [[:en:brooms|brooms]], and earned their income through
peddling and repairs.
In the Meiji period, the Sanka population was estimated at around 200,000, and about 10,000 were thought to remain immediately after World War II. However, these numbers are speculative and have not been verified. The term gained widespread recognition postwar through the fictionalized "Sanka novels" of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]]. These novels popularized Sanka as a subject of intrigue, blending folklore with drama. Writers such as {{ill|Hiroyuki Itsuki|en|Hiroyuki Itsuki|WD=Q1620313|lt=Hiroyuki Itsuki|1=Hiroyuki Itsuki}} further fictionalized the Sanka, incorporating fantastical elements. Movies like ''{{ill|Seburi Monogatari|en|Seburi Monogatari|WD=Q29825842|lt=Seburi Monogatari|1=Seburi Monogatari}}'' (directed by {{ill|Sadao Nakajima|en|Sadao Nakajima|WD=Q7397562|lt=Sadao Nakajima|1=Sadao Nakajima}}) were also inspired by these stories.
The {{ill|Occult|en|Occult|WD=Q178934|lt=Occult|1=Occult}} boom of the 1980s brought renewed interest in the Sanka, with sensational claims linking them to [[:en:kamiyo moji|kamiyo moji]] (ancient script), [[:en:supernatural powers|supernatural powers]], and [[:en:ancient civilizations|ancient civilizations]]. These claims fueled skepticism, leading some to question whether the Sanka ever existed.
== Research == The first academic investigation into the Sanka was conducted by [[Kunio Yanagita]]. Between 1911 and 1912, he published a series of articles titled "Itaka and Sanka" in the journal ''Anthropological Magazine''<ref name="yanagida1">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=6|pages=332–338|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.332}}</ref><ref name="yanagida2">{{Cite journal|author=Kunio Yanagita|title=Itaka and Sanka (Part 2)|journal=Anthropological Magazine|year=1911|volume=27|issue=8|pages=465–471|doi=10.1537/ase1911.27.465}}</ref>. Yanagita criticized earlier theories that equated Sanka with criminality, arguing that their actions reflected differing views on property rather than innate criminality.
Subsequent research, including the work of [[Tsunekata Hasegawa]], contributed to the popular image of the Sanka, though much of it was later revealed to be fictionalized.

{{Citation needed|date=November 2007}} {{Otheruses}} '''Sanka''' (山窩) also known as Japanese Gypsies were a group of itinerant people in Japan who were said to have lived without permanent settlements.<ref>[https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sanka-people Sanka | African, Animist & Nomadic | Britannica]</ref>
== Lifestyle == Sanka were said to have lived a [[:en:hunter-gatherer society|hunter-gatherer]] lifestyle, moving from place to place. They were known for producing [[winnowing baskets]] and would visit villages to trade their goods. There were occupational distinctions within the Sanka community. Those called "Pon" engaged in river fishing and performed secondary tasks such as [[bamboo crafts]]<ref>{{Cite book|author=Tsutsui Isao|title=The Origins of Sanka: From Kugutsu to the Korean Peninsula|publisher=Kawade Shobo Shinsha|year=2012|isbn=978-4-309-22578-4|chapter=1. Ecological Theories of Sanka (Regional Nomenclature and Characteristics)}}</ref>. Another subgroup, referred to as "Minaoshi" or "Tenba," made winnowing baskets, [[:en:Sasara|Sasara]], and [[:en:brooms|brooms]], and earned their income through
peddling and repairs.
In the Meiji period, the Sanka population was estimated at around 200,000, and about 10,000 were thought to remain immediately after World War II. However, these numbers are speculative and have not been verified. Women in Sanka communities reportedly often resorted to prostitution to sustain themselves, leading to the term "Sanka" being associated with prostitutes. While the Sanka predominantly spoke Japanese, they also used a distinct [[Sanka language]] for certain terms.
== Nomenclature == The term "Sanka" was written using various kanji characters, such as 山窩, 山家, 三家, 散家, 傘下, or 燦下. These characters were often phonetic or descriptive, with some suggesting meanings such as "people who live under umbrellas or the sky instead of houses." Regional variations in terminology included "Pon," "Kametsuri," "Minaoshi" (箕直), "Mitsukuri" (箕作), and "Tenba" (転場). These terms often reflected specific trades or practices within the Sanka community.
=== Government and Police Terminology === * '''Government:''' The term "Sanka" was used to categorize itinerants as part of the "vagrants" or "wandering nonpersons" groups. * '''Police:''' The police uniformly referred to them as "Yamaka" (山窩), labeling them as "criminal groups of wandering units." * '''Researchers:''' Scholars used the term "Sanka" distinctly to separate it from police classifications. * '''Forestry Department:''' The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry used "Sanka" or "Yamaka" to document individuals as part of forest preservation efforts against illegal logging.
Some sources suggest that the Sanka referred to themselves as "Kenta" to denote their community. Groups camping by rivers were called "Seburi Kenta," while those with fixed abodes were known as "Doyatsuke Kenta"<ref name="Sanka Self-Naming">{{Cite book|author=Nobuyoshi Wada|title=Dark Street Life: Dictionary of Slang and Symbols|publisher=Toa Shobo|year=1936|url=https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/10297894}}</ref>.
== History of the Term "Sanka" == {{Original research|date=October 2020}} The earliest appearance of the term "Sanka" in records dates to the late {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}. {{ill|Matsuura Takeshirō|en|Matsuura Takeshirō|WD=Q11531839|lt=Matsuura Takeshirō|1=Matsuura Takeshirō}}, an explorer known for naming [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]], recorded being saved by the Sanka in his writings. However, this term was not self-applied by the group, and its use likely predated these documents. In {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|en|Hiroshima Prefecture|WD=Q617375|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|1=Hiroshima Prefecture}}, an 1855 village document used "Sanka" to describe "mountain-dwelling criminals."
During the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}}, "Yamaka" became a term frequently used in police and administrative documents to describe a group akin to [[:en:Bandits|Bandits]].
